name: Upper Guinea Crioulo
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Kihm, Alain. 1994. Kriyol Syntax (Benjamins); Wilson, W.A.A. 1962. The Crioulo of Guinea
earlier_scan.note: APiCS survey ch. 33 read online has no stress section; print grammars plausibly cover it

new_statements.quote: This suggests a very simple rule, for all intents and purposes identical with that which seems to hold in Portuguese, namely: assign stress to the penultimate syllable, unless the ultimate syllable is heavy, in which case it bears stress. A heavy syllable is one that has a realized coda, and the list of possible codas appears to be the same in K and S and in Portuguese, viz. sonorants and approximants (/l/, /r/, /N/, /I/, /U/) and /s/. [p. 3] ... In K and B, in contrast, the syntactic category of the lexical items is a crucial piece of information: nouns are stressed according to their syllable structure; verbs are stressed on their final syllable, irrespective of syllable structure. [p. 5]
new_statements.citation: Andrade, Ernesto d' & Alain Kihm. 2000. Stress in three creoles. In Ernesto d'Andrade, Maria Antónia Mota & Dulce Pereira (eds), Crioulos de base portuguesa, 97-109. Lisboa: Associação Portuguesa de Linguística. (author preprint, 17 pp.)
new_statements.locator: Section 2 'Lexical stress in K, S, and B', preprint pp. 3 and 5 (published pp. 97-109); rule (15) preprint p. 12
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nouns (and other non-verbs): stress the penultimate syllable unless the final syllable has a coda (l, r, nasal, glide, s), in which case the final syllable is stressed (plánta 'plant', minjér 'woman'); verbs take final stress regardless of syllable weight (plantá 'to plant', kumé 'to eat', bambú). A phonological word formed by the 1sg clitic N plus a verb with a prenasalized initial consonant shifts stress to that initial 'left-heavy' syllable (N ntíndi 'I understood' vs. N pañá 'I caught').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by Andrade & Kihm. Chapouto 2014 p. 17 reports Bull 1989 p. 77: trisyllabic nouns stressed on the last syllable carry a secondary stress on the first syllable, and numerals of more than three syllables have main stress on the penult with secondary stress on the first syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: A residue of nouns falls outside the rule (lápis 'pencil', penult despite heavy final; sángra 'hen coop'); plural -s does not make the final syllable heavy (kásas vs. kabás); the initial-stress rule for N + prenasalized verb is stated only for disyllabic verbs. Chapouto 2014 (pp. 41-42, fn. 37, fn. 45) found her Bissau informants conforming to the noun rule but not the verb-final rule (they judged verb stress 'generally penultimate'). Almeida 1991 p. 5 notes that suffixed object pronouns shift stress to the last syllable. Couto 1994 (per Chapouto) entertains a tonal contour for traditional creole.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word) stress; the authors abstract away from its phonetic realization (intensity/pitch/duration), referring to Kihm & Laks 1989 for that. Domain is the phonological word, which includes the proclitic N 'I' and enclitic object pronouns.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Andrade & Kihm 2000, 'K') describes Guinea-Bissau Kriyol proper, i.e. the Bissau-based standard variety (language-level uppe1455; Glottolog dialect biss1249 Bissau-Bolama Creole). The Casamance/Ziguinchor dialect (cach1242 Cacheu-Ziguinchor Creole) is described separately by Biagui & Quint (APiCS ch. 34) as having lexically distinctive stress on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, so the two varieties should not be merged under one stress reading without checking Biagui 2012. Chapouto 2014's Bissau informants also disputed verb-final stress.

sources.locator: Section 2 'Lexical stress in K, S, and B', preprint pp. 3 and 5 (published pp. 97-109); rule (15) preprint p. 12
sources.note: Kriyol (K) nouns: stress on the penult unless the final syllable is heavy (realized coda l, r, N, glide, s), then final; verbs: final stress irrespective of syllable structure; residue nouns like lápis; plural -s does not make a syllable heavy; after the clitic N 'I' a disyllabic verb with prenasalized onset takes initial stress (N ntíndi), formalised as rule (15) p. 12.

sources.citation: Biagui, Noël Bernard & Nicolas Quint. 2013. Casamancese Creole. APiCS Online survey chapter 34.
sources.note: Section 4: 'Casamancese Creole is a stress language. Each content word has a stressed syllable... (1) final: kortá... (2) penultimate: kárgu... (3) antepenultimate: lárguma... Stress has a distinctive function: kónta "(pearl) necklace" vs. kontá "tell"'; open stressed penults are lengthened phonetically. This is the Ziguinchor dialect (Glottolog cach1242).

sources.citation: Almeida, Sabou Espirito Santo Vaz de. 1991. Crioulo Grammar Made Simple. Bissau: Peace Corps. 56 pp. (ERIC ED402736, image-only scan; scanned of pp. 1-10)
sources.note: Pronunciation hints (p. 1) give vowel/consonant values only; p. 5 notes that singular object pronouns and 1pl become verb suffixes 'and the stress shifts to the last syllable' (Parím, ojáu, Falál, Mostrámu); possessive adjectives 'usually are not stressed in a sentence'. No general word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Chapouto, Sandra Marisa da Costa. 2014. Contributo para a descrição de aspetos fonológicos e prosódicos do crioulo guineense. MA thesis, Universidade de Coimbra. 152 pp.
sources.note: Section 1.2.4 Acento (pp. 17-18) is a second-hand synthesis: Bull 1989 pp. 76-78, Andrade et al. 1992 pp. 135-140 and Kihm 1994 p. 14 treat Guineense as a stress language; nouns: penult if last syllable open, final if closed (plural -s excepted); verbs: final (Bull: always; Kihm: when verb ends in a vowel); Bull: trisyllabic final-stressed nouns get secondary stress on the first syllable; numerals >3 syllables main penult + secondary initial; Couto 1994 suggests a tonal contour in traditional creole. Own corpus (fn. 45 p. 57; pp. 41-42 fn. 37): nouns/adjectives conform, verbs did not; two inf…

sources.citation: Couto, Hildo Honório do. 1994. O crioulo português da Guiné-Bissau. Hamburg: Helmut Buske. (Rosetta Project excerpts: phonology pp. 68-73, texts pp. 136-139)
sources.note: The open excerpt covers only consonants (3.1.1) and vowels (3.1.2); nothing on stress in these pages. Per Chapouto 2014 p. 17, Couto's full chapter suggests a tonal contour in traditional creole and stress mainly in the lusitanised variety.

sources.citation: Costa, Paula Mendes. 2014. Descrição fonológica do crioulo guineense. MA thesis, Universidade Federal de Pernambuco. 242 pp.
sources.note: Segmental phonology and syllable only; marks tonic syllables in transcriptions and distributes allophones by tonicity (pretonic/tonic/posttonic) but states no rule for stress placement.

sources.citation: Intumbo, Incanha, Sandra Chapouto & John Holm. 2013. Guinea-Bissau Kriyol. APiCS Online survey chapter 33 (Michaelis et al. eds, Survey of pidgin and creole languages vol. 2, OUP).
sources.note: No mention of stress, accent or tone anywhere in the chapter (confirms the earlier scan note).
